paras: The lynching at Refugio, Texas, was the killing of an unnamed Black man by a mob in late February or early March 1881, after he was accused of raping a white woman. He was taken from the jail and, according to the Memphis Appeal, hanged. The case survives only as a short exchange paragraph reprinted in Tennessee and Texas papers, one of which called his death "deserved."

According to the Memphis Appeal of March 4, "last week" a Black man "ravished a white lady at Refugio, Texas, whose name is withheld." The woman was said to have followed him a mile trying to kill him with an ax, but he escaped. He was later captured and jailed.

In the Memphis Appeal's words, "A mob took him out and hung him." The Texas version said only that he was "taken from jail by force, to meet a deserved and violent death," without naming the method or the place where he was killed. Neither account gives his name, the date of the lynching, or the number or identity of the men who took him.
No report of an inquest, arrests, or other official response appears in the coverage.

The Memphis Appeal printed the story on March 4 as one line in its "Notes from our Neighbors" column, among items on Arkansas schools, Alabama cotton mills, and Texas court news. It called the accused "The brute" but added no comment on the mob.

In Texas the Austin Weekly Democratic Statesman ran a slightly different paragraph on March 10 that called the man "the brute" and the woman "outraged," and endorsed the killing as "deserved." The Dallas Daily Herald reprinted that paragraph almost word for word in its "Texas Topics" column on March 24.

reader.title: Lynching at Refugio, Texas (1881)
bases: A mob took an accused Black man from the Refugio jail and killed him (A1, A2).

The Memphis Appeal says 'a mob' took the jailed man out and hanged him, and the Austin Statesman says he was taken from jail 'by force' to a 'violent death' (A1, A2); the pretext was the accusation that he had raped a white woman (A1, A2).

The two independent-looking reports (A1, A2) are short exchange paragraphs with the same sequence of details and no local byline, and the Dallas item (A3) reprints A2, so the episode rests on one untraced Texas item.
